newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Farm ministers face marathon beef package talks.
newsitem.headline: Farm ministers face marathon beef package talks.

text.p: Farm ministers face a marathon three day meeting from Monday when they meet to thrash out measures to combat the impact of the mad cow crisis on farmers and the markets, EU diplomats said on Friday.
"Member states are divided on almost every issue on this part of the agenda and it is hard to see how the impasse will be resolved," one diplomat said.
The Irish EU Presidency said it planned to present a possible compromise paper on Tuesday morning following a table round discussion on Monday.
"But it will be very difficult to achieve an agreement," an Irish official said, adding talks could continue into Wednesday.
Some diplomats and Commission sources suggested that a deal could be struck on a mini-package containing measures having the most immediate impact.
This would include increased purchases into intervention and inclusion of young male cattle plus extension of a calf slaughtering scheme to all member states.

Little progress has been made despite instructions from farm ministers at an informal meeting in Killarney, Ireland, in September to resolve disagreements over Commisssion proposals presented on July 30 to change beef market Regulation 805/68:
The proposals, intended to rebalance the market after the Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE) crisis, were for:
- An increase in beef intervention ceilings to 720,000 tonnes in 1996 and 500,000 tonnes in 1997.
- Extending the beef intervention scheme to cover young male cattle of between seven and nine months of age less than 300 kg liveweight.
- All member states to offer aid to farmers to slaughter calves up to 20 days of age.
- Abolition of the second premium for young bulls and increase in size of first premium
- Reduction of cattle stocking density to 1.2 cattle per hectare, from 1.4 cattle as an incentive for more extensive farming.
- Reduction in number of male cattle eligible for beef premium payments.
The proposals are designed to bring the beef market back into balance and to finance the 1.3 billion Ecu cost of the mad cow crisis.

The package would be financed by a controversial plan to cut arable area payments and set aside compensation provided under Regulation 1765/92, which only Britain and Sweden have so far indicated any support.
Aid payments to cereals and oilseeds farmers due in 1996 would also be postponed until 1997.
As the European Parliament has not yet given an opinion on the financing proposal, farm ministers cannot take any formal decision.
The same applies to a Commission proposal changing investment rules in the livestock sector.
Diplomats said it would be difficult for countries such as France and Germany to agree beef production-cutting measures without a corresponding aid package.

Germany has proposed a different approach which would introduce incentives to beef producers to slaughter animals earlier and at lighter weights, selling the meat onto themarket rather than into intervention stores.
This would eliminate the calf processing scheme which is called the 'Herod scheme' because it pays farmers to have calves slaughtered before they are 20 days old.
"This is something that is unacceptable to some member states and it has raised much controversy," the diplomat said.
But the Commission says the German scheme would be expensive, difficult to control and not cut production further than its own proposals.
France on the other hand wants more aid for beef producers and would like to see the so called Herod scheme extended.
